## Overview

Diffusion and flow models generate a sample by integrating an ordinary
differential equation (ODE) from a simple distribution to the data
distribution. Every sample therefore costs tens or hundreds of network
evaluations. The first part of this lecture block looked at early ways around
that cost (progressive distillation, denoising diffusion GANs). This lecture
gives the general theory behind the modern few-step and one-step generators,
and then reads three concrete methods through that theory.

The idea is to stop learning the *velocity* of the ODE and to learn its
*solution operator* instead. A velocity field tells us where a point moves in an
infinitesimal time; the **flow map** $X_{s,t}$ tells us where a point that is
at $x$ at time $s$ will be at time $t$, for any pair $(s,t)$. A network that
represents the flow map can jump from noise to data in one evaluation.

The lecture has two parts, and the note follows them in order.

1. **Flow maps: theory.** We set up *stochastic interpolants*, a single
   framework that contains both flow matching and diffusion models, and recall
   how the velocity $b$ is learned by regression. We then define the flow map,
   see why learning it directly from its definition is inefficient, and derive
   two differential characterizations of it, the *Lagrangian* and the
   *Eulerian* equation. Each one gives a distillation loss (LMD and EMD) and a
   derivative-free discrete version of it (DLMD and DEMD).
2. **Flow map training in practice.** Consistency models (CM), latent
   consistency models (LCM) and consistency trajectory models (CTM) are shown
   to be instances of the discrete Eulerian loss with a stop-gradient. CTM
   additionally reveals that a flow map contains a flow matching model on its
   diagonal $s=t$, which is what stabilizes training.

After reading the note you should be able to (i) state and prove why the
regression loss recovers the probability flow velocity, (ii) derive the
Lagrangian and Eulerian equations and prove that each one characterizes the
flow map, (iii) show that the discrete losses converge to the continuous ones,
and (iv) explain CM, LCM and CTM as special cases, including what the
stop-gradient and the flow matching term are for.

The derivations that the slides state without proof, or leave as an exercise,
are carried out in full: the proofs of @prp-pf, @prp-learn and @prp-suff, the
convergence of the discrete Eulerian loss (@prp-eulerconv), the fixed point of the
stop-gradient loss (@prp-fixed), the reduction of consistency training to a
teacher-free loss (@prp-ct), and the slide exercise that the Eulerian loss
becomes flow matching in the limit $t \to s$ (@prp-fm-limit). A worked example
with a closed-form flow map and runnable code is in @sec-ch15-worked.

## Notation

The notation is that of the lecture slides. Time runs over $[0,1]$.

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $p_0, p_1$ | the two probability densities on $\mathbb{R}^d$ we want to translate between |
| $x_0 \sim p_0,\ x_1 \sim p_1,\ z \sim \mathcal{N}(0,I)$ | endpoint samples and an independent Gaussian latent variable |
| $I_t$ | stochastic interpolant, $I_t = \alpha_t x_0 + \beta_t x_1 + \gamma_t z$ |
| $\dot{I}_t$ | time derivative of the interpolant, $\dot\alpha_t x_0 + \dot\beta_t x_1 + \dot\gamma_t z$ |
| $\rho_t$ | probability density of $I_t$ (so $\rho_0 = p_0$, $\rho_1 = p_1$) |
| $b_t(x)$ | velocity field, $b_t(x) = \mathbb{E}[\dot{I}_t \mid I_t = x]$ |
| $\hat{b}$ | a candidate (learned) velocity field |
| $(x_t)_{t \in [0,1]}$ | a solution of the ODE $\dot{x}_t = b_t(x_t)$ |
| $X_{s,t}$ | flow map: $X_{s,t}(x_s) = x_t$ |
| $\hat{X}_{s,t}$ | a candidate (learned) flow map |
| $\nabla X_{s,t}(x)$ | Jacobian of $x \mapsto X_{s,t}(x)$, a $d \times d$ matrix |
| $\partial_s, \partial_t$ | partial derivatives in the start time $s$ and the destination time $t$ |
| $w_{s,t} > 0$ | a positive weight on the pair $(s,t)$ |
| $\mathrm{ODESolve}_{s,t}(x)$ | the result of numerically integrating $\dot{x} = b(x)$ from time $s$ to time $t$, started at $x$ |
| $\mathrm{sg}[\cdot]$ | stop-gradient: the argument is treated as a constant when differentiating the loss |
| $X_s$ | consistency model, $X_s = X_{s,1}$ |
| $F_{s,t}$ | average velocity in the parametrization $X_{s,t}(x) = x + (t-s)F_{s,t}(x)$ |
| NFE | number of function (network) evaluations used to draw one sample |

Two conventions deserve a warning. First, the expression
$b_s(x) \cdot \nabla X_{s,t}(x)$ on the slides means the directional
derivative of $X_{s,t}$ along $b_s(x)$, that is the matrix-vector product
$\nabla X_{s,t}(x)\, b_s(x)$. Second, the slides do not fix which of $p_0$ and
$p_1$ is the data distribution, because the theory is symmetric in time:
$X_{s,t}$ is defined for $s<t$ and for $s>t$. When a direction is needed, the
consistency model of @def-cm takes time $1$ as the destination, so there $p_1$
plays the role of data and $p_0$ of noise.

## Stochastic Interpolants

### Definition and examples

We want to translate between two distributions $p_0$ and $p_1$, for instance
from noise to images or from one image domain to another. The starting point is
to connect a sample of $p_0$ and a sample of $p_1$ by an explicit path.

::: {#def-interpolant}
## Stochastic interpolant (slide Definition 1)
A *stochastic interpolant* between probability densities $p_0$ and $p_1$ is the
stochastic process
$$
I_t = \alpha_t x_0 + \beta_t x_1 + \gamma_t z,
\qquad x_0 \sim p_0,\quad x_1 \sim p_1,\quad z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I),
$$ {#eq-interpolant}
for $t \in [0,1]$, where $z$ is independent of $(x_0,x_1)$ and the scalar
coefficients satisfy
$$
\alpha_0 = \beta_1 = 1, \qquad \alpha_1 = \beta_0 = 0, \qquad \gamma_0 = \gamma_1 = 0 .
$$
:::

The boundary conditions say exactly that $I_0 = x_0 \sim p_0$ and
$I_1 = x_1 \sim p_1$. In between, $I_t$ is a random point whose density we call
$\rho_t$; the family $(\rho_t)_{t\in[0,1]}$ is a path of densities from $p_0$
to $p_1$. We assume throughout that $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ are continuous on
$[0,1]$ and differentiable on the open interval $(0,1)$, so that
$\dot{I}_t = \dot\alpha_t x_0 + \dot\beta_t x_1 + \dot\gamma_t z$ exists for
$0<t<1$. (Differentiability at the endpoints would be too much to ask: for
$\gamma_t = \sqrt{2t(1-t)}$, used below, $\dot\gamma_t$ is unbounded as
$t\to0$ and $t\to1$.) The pair $(x_0,x_1)$ may be drawn from any coupling of $p_0$ and $p_1$;
the simplest choice, used in the examples below, is to draw them independently.

The slides show four choices of coefficients, each visualized as a sequence of
images going from a daisy ($x_0$) to a passion flower ($x_1$):

| Name on the slide | Interpolant | What the path looks like |
|---|---|---|
| Without latent variable | $x_t = (1-t)x_0 + t x_1$ | a cross-fade of the two images |
| With latent variable | $x_t = (1-t)x_0 + t x_1 + \sqrt{2t(1-t)}\, z$ | a cross-fade with extra noise that peaks at $t = 1/2$ |
| Gaussian encoding-decoding | $x_t = \cos^2(\pi t)\big(1_{[0,1/2)}(t)\, x_0 + 1_{(1/2,1]}(t)\, x_1\big) + \sqrt{2t(1-t)}\, z$ | $x_0$ is destroyed into pure noise at $t = 1/2$, then $x_1$ is created from it |
| One-sided | $x_t = (1-t) x_0 + t z$ | the image is turned into noise; $p_1 = \mathcal{N}(0,I)$ |

The second and third rows show what the latent variable $z$ is for: it adds
randomness in the middle of the path that is present at neither endpoint. In
the third row $\cos^2(\pi/2) = 0$, so at $t = 1/2$ the interpolant is the pure
noise $z/\sqrt{2}$ and carries no information about either endpoint.

Two special cases cover the models of the previous lectures.

* **Flow model.** $I_t = (1-t)x_0 + t x_1$, that is $\alpha_t = 1-t$,
  $\beta_t = t$, $\gamma_t = 0$. This is the linear interpolation path of flow
  matching and rectified flow.
* **DDPM.** $I_t = \sqrt{\alpha_t}\, x_0 + \sqrt{1-\alpha_t}\, z$. Here, and only
  here, $\alpha_t$ denotes the cumulative noise schedule of DDPM (usually
  written $\bar\alpha_t$), not the interpolant coefficient
  of @def-interpolant. In the language of @def-interpolant this is a one-sided
  interpolant with $x_0$ the data, $p_1 = \mathcal{N}(0,I)$ and $x_1 = z$:
  the coefficient of $x_0$ is $\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}$ and the coefficient of
  $x_1$ is $\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}$, with the diffusion time rescaled to
  $[0,1]$. The boundary conditions hold because $\bar\alpha = 1$ at the data
  end and $\bar\alpha \approx 0$ at the noise end.

::: {.callout-important}
## Emphasized in the lecture
All subsequent theory holds for diffusion **and** flow models. Everything
below is stated for a general interpolant and uses only the velocity $b$, so
the same flow map theory applies to both families.
:::

### The probability flow ODE

The interpolant is easy to sample but it is not a generative model: to produce
$I_t$ we need both endpoints. The next result replaces the interpolant by a
deterministic ODE that has the same marginal densities and needs only one
endpoint.

::: {#prp-pf}
## Probability flow (slide Proposition 1)
For all $t \in [0,1]$, the probability density of $I_t$ is the same as the
probability density of the solution to the ODE
$$
\dot{x}_t = b_t(x_t), \qquad x_{t=0} = x_0 \sim p_0 \quad \text{or} \quad x_{t=1} = x_1 \sim p_1,
$$ {#eq-pfode}
where $b$ is the velocity given by
$$
b_t(x) = \mathbb{E}[\dot{I}_t \mid I_t = x]
       = \mathbb{E}[\dot\alpha_t x_0 + \dot\beta_t x_1 + \dot\gamma_t z \mid I_t = x].
$$ {#eq-velocity}
:::

The slide states this without proof. The proof below assumes that, for
$t\in(0,1)$, $I_t$ has a density $\rho_t$ that is differentiable in $t$ and
continuous up to $t=0$ and $t=1$, that $\mathbb{E}\|\dot{I}_t\| < \infty$, and
that $b_t(x)$ is continuous in $t$ and locally Lipschitz in $x$ with at most
linear growth, so that the ODE @eq-pfode has a unique solution through every
point. The continuity equation below is understood in the weak sense, that is,
tested against smooth functions; no differentiability of $\rho_t$ in $x$ is
needed.

::: {.proof}
*Step 1: $\rho_t$ solves a continuity equation.* Let
$\varphi : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}$ be a smooth test function with compact
support. By the chain rule and then the tower property of conditional
expectation,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d}{dt} \mathbb{E}[\varphi(I_t)]
  &= \mathbb{E}\big[\nabla\varphi(I_t) \cdot \dot{I}_t\big]
   = \mathbb{E}\Big[\nabla\varphi(I_t) \cdot \mathbb{E}[\dot{I}_t \mid I_t]\Big] \\
  &= \mathbb{E}\big[\nabla\varphi(I_t) \cdot b_t(I_t)\big]
   = \int \nabla\varphi(x) \cdot b_t(x)\, \rho_t(x)\, dx .
\end{aligned}
$$
The left-hand side is $\int \varphi(x)\, \partial_t \rho_t(x)\, dx$.
Integrating the right-hand side by parts (the boundary term vanishes because
$\varphi$ has compact support) gives
$-\int \varphi(x)\, \nabla \cdot (b_t(x)\rho_t(x))\, dx$. Since $\varphi$ is
arbitrary, this is the weak form of
$$
\partial_t \rho_t + \nabla \cdot (b_t \rho_t) = 0 , \qquad \rho_0 = p_0,\quad \rho_1 = p_1 .
$$ {#eq-continuity}

*Step 2: the ODE solution solves the same equation.* Let $x_t$ solve
@eq-pfode with $x_0 \sim p_0$ and let $q_t$ be the density of $x_t$. The same
computation, now with $\dot{x}_t = b_t(x_t)$ in place of $\dot{I}_t$, gives
$\frac{d}{dt}\mathbb{E}[\varphi(x_t)] = \mathbb{E}[\nabla\varphi(x_t)\cdot b_t(x_t)]$,
hence $\partial_t q_t + \nabla\cdot(b_t q_t) = 0$ with $q_0 = p_0$.

*Step 3: uniqueness.* Under the regularity assumed for $b$, the continuity
equation with velocity $b$ has a unique solution for a given initial density
(it is the push-forward of the initial density by the flow of the ODE).
Therefore $q_t = \rho_t$ for all $t$. Starting instead from $x_1 \sim p_1$ and
integrating backward in time is the same argument with the terminal condition
$\rho_1 = p_1$.
:::

The proposition does **not** say that the ODE trajectories are the interpolant
trajectories. Only the one-time marginals agree. The slide illustrates the
difference with two panels, reproduced with a one-dimensional example
in @fig-interp. The paths $t \mapsto I_t$ are straight lines between independently
drawn endpoints and they cross each other. At a crossing point $x$ several
different values of $\dot{I}_t$ occur, and $b_t(x)$ is their average. The ODE
replaces the bundle of crossing paths by a single deterministic direction at
each point, so its solutions cannot cross (two solutions that meet would
coincide by uniqueness), and the map from start to end becomes a deterministic
transport.

![Interpolant paths versus ODE solutions for $p_0 = \mathcal{N}(0,1)$ and a
two-component Gaussian mixture $p_1$, with $I_t = (1-t)x_0 + t x_1$ and
independent endpoints. Color marks the mixture component the path ends in.
Left: the paths of $I_t$ cross (two of them are drawn in black), so a point
$(t,x)$ does not determine where a path is going. Right: solutions of
$\dot{x}_t = b_t(x_t)$ from the same starting points never cross, yet at every
$t$ the two panels have the same density of points (@prp-pf).](figures/lec15/ChungEunho-interpolant-vs-ode.png){#fig-interp width=95%}

### Learning the velocity

The velocity $b_t(x)$ in @eq-velocity is a conditional expectation and has no
closed form in general. It can however be learned from samples of the
interpolant alone.

::: {#prp-learn}
## Learning flows (slide Proposition 2)
The velocity $b$ can be learned by solving the regression
$$
b = \arg\min_{\hat{b}} \int_0^1 \mathbb{E}\big[\|\hat{b}(I_t) - \dot{I}_t\|^2\big]\, dt ,
$$ {#eq-regression}
where $\mathbb{E}$ is the expectation over $x_0 \sim p_0$, $x_1 \sim p_1$,
$z \sim \mathcal{N}(0,I)$, and $\hat{b}(I_t)$ is short for $\hat{b}_t(I_t)$.
:::

The proof is again not on the slides. It assumes
$\mathbb{E}\|\dot{I}_t\|^2 < \infty$, and the minimum is taken over
candidates with $\mathbb{E}\|\hat{b}_t(I_t)\|^2 < \infty$.

::: {.proof}
Fix $t$ and add and subtract $b_t(I_t)$ inside the norm:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}\|\hat{b}_t(I_t) - \dot{I}_t\|^2
 &= \mathbb{E}\|\hat{b}_t(I_t) - b_t(I_t)\|^2
  + \mathbb{E}\|b_t(I_t) - \dot{I}_t\|^2 \\
 &\quad + 2\, \mathbb{E}\big[(\hat{b}_t(I_t) - b_t(I_t)) \cdot (b_t(I_t) - \dot{I}_t)\big].
\end{aligned}
$$
In the cross term, condition on $I_t$. The first factor is a function of $I_t$
and comes out of the conditional expectation, and
$\mathbb{E}[b_t(I_t) - \dot{I}_t \mid I_t] = b_t(I_t) - b_t(I_t) = 0$ by the
definition @eq-velocity. So the cross term vanishes and
$$
\mathbb{E}\|\hat{b}_t(I_t) - \dot{I}_t\|^2
 = \underbrace{\mathbb{E}\|\hat{b}_t(I_t) - b_t(I_t)\|^2}_{\geq 0,\ \text{zero iff } \hat{b}_t = b_t\ \rho_t\text{-a.e.}}
 + \underbrace{\mathbb{E}\|b_t(I_t) - \dot{I}_t\|^2}_{\text{does not depend on } \hat{b}} .
$$ {#eq-decomp}
Integrating over $t$, the objective is minimized exactly when
$\hat{b}_t = b_t$ almost everywhere with respect to $\rho_t$, for almost every
$t$.
:::

The picture on the slide shows one point $I_t$ with a fan of dotted arrows
$\dot{I}_t$ (one for each pair of endpoints whose path passes through that
point) and one solid arrow $b(I_t) = \mathbb{E}[\dot{I}_t \mid I_t]$, their
average. Two remarks from the lecture annotate the formula. The network input
$I_t$ is a sample from the *marginal* density $\rho_t$, which is easy to draw.
The regression target $\dot{I}_t$ is a single sample of the conditional
velocity, which is noisy; the conditional mean $b$ itself is intractable, but
@eq-decomp shows that regressing on the noisy target has the same minimizer,
and that the minimum value of the loss is not zero but the conditional
variance $\int_0^1\mathbb{E}\|b_t(I_t) - \dot{I}_t\|^2 dt$.

::: {#cor-fm}
## Flow matching (slide Corollary 2.1)
The flow ODE with $I_t = (1-t)x_0 + t x_1$ can be learned by
$$
b = \arg\min_{\hat{b}} \int_0^1 \mathbb{E}\big[\|\hat{b}(I_t) - (x_1 - x_0)\|^2\big]\, dt ,
$$ {#eq-fm}
that is, by solving the flow matching loss.
:::

::: {.proof}
For $\alpha_t = 1-t$, $\beta_t = t$, $\gamma_t = 0$ we have
$\dot{I}_t = x_1 - x_0$. Substitute into @eq-regression.
:::

## Flow Maps

The ODE @eq-pfode turns a sample of $p_0$ into a sample of $p_1$, but only
after many small solver steps, each of which evaluates the network $\hat{b}$.
To generate in one or a few steps we want the solution of the ODE itself as a
function.

::: {#def-flowmap}
## Flow map (slide Definition 2)
A *flow map* $X_{s,t} : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d$ is the unique map such
that
$$
X_{s,t}(x_s) = x_t \qquad \forall (s,t) \in [0,1]^2 ,
$$ {#eq-flowmap}
where $(x_t)_{t\in[0,1]}$ is any solution to the ODE $\dot{x}_t = b_t(x_t)$.
:::

In words: $X_{s,t}$ takes the position at the *starting time* $s$ of any ODE
trajectory and returns the position of the same trajectory at the
*destination time* $t$. It is a function of two time variables. The slide
contrasts the two objects with a figure: flow matching learns a tangent
$v_\theta(x_t,t)$ at each point of a trajectory, a flow map learns the jump
$x_s \mapsto x_t$ between any two points of it. In the words of the lecture, a
flow map learns *all the geometry of the transitions*: one network knows every
transition $s \to t$ at once.

The following consequences of @def-flowmap and of the uniqueness of ODE
solutions are not stated as a result on the slides, but they are used
repeatedly below (for instance in the multi-step sampler of @sec-ctm), so we
record them.

::: {#prp-ch15-semigroup}
## Elementary properties of the flow map
For all $s,u,t \in [0,1]$ and $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$:

1. $X_{s,s}(x) = x$ (identity on the diagonal);
2. $X_{u,t}(X_{s,u}(x)) = X_{s,t}(x)$ (composition);
3. $X_{t,s} = X_{s,t}^{-1}$ (inverse);
4. if $x_0 \sim p_0$ then $X_{0,t}(x_0) \sim \rho_t$; in particular
   $X_{0,1}(x_0) \sim p_1$, a one-step sampler.
:::

::: {.proof}
Let $(x_\tau)$ be the solution with $x_s = x$. (1) $X_{s,s}(x_s) = x_s$.
(2) $X_{s,u}(x) = x_u$ and $X_{u,t}(x_u) = x_t = X_{s,t}(x)$. (3) Take $t = s$
in (2) with the roles of $s,u$ exchanged. (4) $X_{0,t}(x_0) = x_t$, whose
density is $\rho_t$ by @prp-pf.
:::

### The obvious approach and why it is inefficient

How do we learn a flow map? The lecture first considers the obvious approach,
written on the slide for the map from time $1$ to time $0$:

1. sample a lot of $x_1 \sim p_1$ (say $N$ points);
2. solve the ODE $\dot{x}_t = b(x_t)$ with a large number of discretization
   steps to get $x_0$;
3. optimize the flow map by
$$
\min_{X} \frac{1}{N} \sum_{n=1}^{N} d\big(x_0^{(n)}, X_{1,0}(x_1^{(n)})\big),
$$ {#eq-naive}
where $d$ is any loss function (for example the mean squared error, MSE, or
the perceptual distance LPIPS) and $(x_1^{(n)}, x_0^{(n)})$ is the $n$-th pair
of ODE endpoints. (The slide omits the sample index $n$; it is added here.)

This is regression on the definition @eq-flowmap itself. It is correct, but
*trying to optimize a flow map using the definition itself was inefficient*:
every training pair requires a complete, accurate ODE solve with the given
velocity $b$, so building the training set costs as much as running the slow sampler
$N$ times, and the pairs only supervise one pair of times, $(s,t) = (1,0)$.
The question that organizes the rest of the lecture is therefore:

> Why not try using the first-order derivative of the definition?

A derivative of @eq-flowmap is a *local* condition. It can be checked at a
single time pair with a single evaluation of $b$, without solving the ODE.

## Flow Map Distillation

### Lagrangian and Eulerian equations

The definition $X_{s,t}(x_s) = x_t$ contains two time variables, and we can
differentiate it with respect to either. The slide states the two results; the
computations are as follows.

**Derivative with respect to $t$.** Fix $s$ and a trajectory $(x_\tau)$.
Differentiating $X_{s,t}(x_s) = x_t$ in $t$ gives
$\partial_t X_{s,t}(x_s) = \dot{x}_t = b_t(x_t) = b_t(X_{s,t}(x_s))$. Since a
trajectory passes through every point $x$ at time $s$, we may write $x$ for
$x_s$:
$$
\partial_t X_{s,t}(x) = b_t(X_{s,t}(x)), \qquad X_{s,s}(x) = x .
$$ {#eq-lagrangian}

**Derivative with respect to $s$.** Fix $t$ and differentiate
$X_{s,t}(x_s) = x_t$ in $s$. The right-hand side does not depend on $s$. On the
left, $s$ appears twice, in the index and in the argument $x_s$, so by the
chain rule
$$
0 = \frac{d}{ds}\big[X_{s,t}(x_s)\big]
  = \partial_s X_{s,t}(x_s) + \nabla X_{s,t}(x_s)\, \dot{x}_s
  = \partial_s X_{s,t}(x_s) + \nabla X_{s,t}(x_s)\, b_s(x_s) .
$$
Writing $x$ for $x_s$ again, and using the slide notation
$b_s(x)\cdot\nabla X_{s,t}(x)$ for $\nabla X_{s,t}(x)\,b_s(x)$,
$$
\partial_s X_{s,t}(x) + b_s(x) \cdot \nabla X_{s,t}(x) = 0, \qquad X_{t,t}(x) = x .
$$ {#eq-eulerian}

The names come from fluid mechanics. @eq-lagrangian follows one particle as the
destination time advances: it is the ODE itself, with $X_{s,t}(x)$ as the
moving particle. @eq-eulerian keeps the destination fixed and asks how the
answer changes when the starting point is moved; it is a linear transport
equation in the variables $(s,x)$, and it says that $X_{s,t}(\cdot)$ is
constant along trajectories.

We derived the two equations as *necessary* conditions. The key fact is that
each of them is also *sufficient*.

::: {#prp-suff}
## Sufficient condition for flow maps (slide Proposition 3)
$X_{s,t}$ is a flow map if it satisfies the *Lagrangian equation* or the
*Eulerian equation* for all $(s,t,x) \in [0,1]^2 \times \mathbb{R}^d$:

* Lagrangian equation: $\partial_t X_{s,t}(x) = b_t(X_{s,t}(x))$, $\ X_{s,s}(x) = x$;
* Eulerian equation: $\partial_s X_{s,t}(x) + b_s(x)\cdot\nabla X_{s,t}(x) = 0$, $\ X_{t,t}(x) = x$.
:::

The slide gives no proof. We assume, as in @prp-pf, that the ODE has a unique
solution through every point, and that the candidate $X$ is continuously
differentiable in $(s,t,x)$.

::: {.proof}
Let $(x_\tau)_{\tau\in[0,1]}$ be any solution of $\dot{x}_\tau = b_\tau(x_\tau)$.
We must show $X_{s,t}(x_s) = x_t$.

*Lagrangian case.* Fix $s$ and define the curve $y_t = X_{s,t}(x_s)$.
By @eq-lagrangian, $\dot{y}_t = b_t(y_t)$ and $y_s = X_{s,s}(x_s) = x_s$. So
$(y_t)$ and $(x_t)$ solve the same ODE and agree at time $s$. By uniqueness
they agree at all times: $X_{s,t}(x_s) = y_t = x_t$.

*Eulerian case.* Fix $t$ and define $g(s) = X_{s,t}(x_s)$. By the chain rule
and @eq-eulerian,
$$
g'(s) = \partial_s X_{s,t}(x_s) + \nabla X_{s,t}(x_s)\, b_s(x_s) = 0 .
$$
So $g$ is constant in $s$, and its value is obtained at $s = t$ from the
boundary condition: $g(s) = g(t) = X_{t,t}(x_t) = x_t$. Hence
$X_{s,t}(x_s) = x_t$.
:::

Note the different roles of the boundary conditions. In the Lagrangian
equation the identity is imposed at the start of the jump, in the Eulerian
equation at its end; both say $X_{s,s} = \mathrm{id}$, but the Eulerian
argument *propagates* that information from $s = t$ back to all other $s$.
This will matter when we discuss the stop-gradient.

### Lagrangian and Eulerian map distillation

A differential equation that characterizes the flow map can be turned into a
loss: penalize the squared residual of the equation. Because the residual
involves the velocity $b$, which in practice is a pre-trained diffusion or
flow model (the *teacher*), this is a *distillation* of the teacher into a
flow map (the *student*).

::: {#cor-fmd}
## Flow map distillation (slide Corollary 3.1)
The flow map is a global minimizer of the losses

* Lagrangian Map Distillation:
$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LMD}}(\hat{X}) = \mathbb{E}_{s,t\in[0,1]}\Big[w_{s,t}\, \mathbb{E}\big[\|\partial_t \hat{X}_{s,t}(I_s) - b_t(\hat{X}_{s,t}(I_s))\|^2\big]\Big],
$$ {#eq-lmd}
* Eulerian Map Distillation:
$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{EMD}}(\hat{X}) = \mathbb{E}_{s,t\in[0,1]}\Big[w_{s,t}\, \mathbb{E}\big[\|\partial_s \hat{X}_{s,t}(I_s) + b_s(I_s)\cdot\nabla\hat{X}_{s,t}(I_s)\|^2\big]\Big],
$$ {#eq-emd}

subject to $\hat{X}_{s,s}(x) = x$ for all $(s,x) \in [0,1]\times\mathbb{R}^d$,
with $w_{s,t} > 0$.
:::

Here the outer expectation draws the pair $(s,t)$ from a distribution on
$[0,1]^2$ (for example uniformly), and the inner expectation draws the point at
which the equation is tested, $I_s \sim \rho_s$, from the interpolant.

::: {.proof}
Both losses are expectations of non-negative quantities, so they are bounded
below by $0$. The true flow map $X$ satisfies the constraint and, by
@eq-lagrangian and @eq-eulerian, makes both residuals vanish identically, so
it attains the value $0$ and is a global minimizer.

Conversely, suppose $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LMD}}(\hat{X}) = 0$ or
$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{EMD}}(\hat{X}) = 0$, and assume in addition that the
pair $(s,t)$ has a positive density on $[0,1]^2$, that $\rho_s > 0$ everywhere,
and that the residual is continuous in $(s,t,x)$. Then the residual, being
zero almost everywhere and continuous, is zero everywhere, and @prp-suff shows
that $\hat{X}$ is the flow map. Under these assumptions the flow map is the
*unique* minimizer.
:::

The constraint $\hat{X}_{s,s} = \mathrm{id}$ cannot be dropped: for example
any $\hat{X}_{s,t}(x)$ that is constant in $(s,x)$ has zero Eulerian residual.
In practice it is built into the network, as in the parametrization
$\hat{X}_{s,t}(x) = x + (t-s)\hat{F}_{s,t}(x)$ of @sec-ctm.

### Discrete version

The losses @eq-lmd and @eq-emd contain derivatives of the network with respect
to its time inputs and, for EMD, a Jacobian-vector product. Replacing the
derivatives by finite differences gives losses that only need forward
evaluations of $\hat{X}$ and one short solver step of the teacher.

::: {#cor-discrete}
## Flow map distillation, discrete variant (slide Corollary 3.2)
The following losses converge to Lagrangian / Eulerian Map Distillation as
$\delta \to 0$:

* Discrete LMD:
$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DLMD}}(\hat{X}) = \mathbb{E}_{s,t\in[0,1]}\Big[w_{s,t}\, \mathbb{E}\big[\|\hat{X}_{s,t}(I_s) - \mathrm{ODESolve}_{t-\delta,t}(\hat{X}_{s,t-\delta}(I_s))\|^2\big]\Big],
$$ {#eq-dlmd}
* Discrete EMD:
$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DEMD}}(\hat{X}) = \mathbb{E}_{s,t\in[0,1]}\Big[w_{s,t}\, \mathbb{E}\big[\|\hat{X}_{s,t}(I_s) - \hat{X}_{s+\delta,t}(\mathrm{ODESolve}_{s,s+\delta}(I_s))\|^2\big]\Big],
$$ {#eq-demd}

subject to $\hat{X}_{s,s}(x) = x$ for all $(s,x) \in [0,1]\times\mathbb{R}^d$,
with $w_{s,t} > 0$.
:::

Here $\delta > 0$ is a small step, and the pair $(s,t)$ is restricted so that
the shifted times $t-\delta$ and $s+\delta$ stay in $[0,1]$; the slides do not
spell this out. The precise meaning of "converge", made explicit by the proof on the slide, is
that $\delta^{-2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DLMD}} \to \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LMD}}$
and $\delta^{-2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DEMD}} \to \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{EMD}}$:
the discrete losses themselves tend to zero like $\delta^2$, and the rescaled
losses tend to the continuous ones. The factor $\delta^{-2}$ is a constant and
does not change the minimizer.

Both proofs use one property of the solver: over a step of length $\delta$ it
agrees with an Euler step up to second order,
$$
\mathrm{ODESolve}_{u,u+\delta}(y) = y + \delta\, b_u(y) + O(\delta^2) .
$$ {#eq-euler-step}
This holds with no remainder if the solver *is* one Euler step, and with an
$O(\delta^2)$ remainder for the exact solution $X_{u,u+\delta}$ and for any
consistent higher-order solver. We assume that $\hat{X}$ is twice continuously
differentiable in $(s,t,x)$, that $b$ is continuously differentiable, and that
the remainders are dominated by an integrable function, so that the limit can
be taken inside the expectations.

::: {.proof}
*Discrete LMD (the proof on the slide, with the remainders written out).*
Abbreviate $y_\delta = \hat{X}_{s,t-\delta}(I_s)$. Then
$$
\begin{aligned}
\delta^{-2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DLMD}}(\hat{X})
 &= \delta^{-2}\,\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\Big[w_{s,t}\,\mathbb{E}\big[\|\hat{X}_{s,t}(I_s) - \mathrm{ODESolve}_{t-\delta,t}(y_\delta)\|^2\big]\Big] \\
 &= \mathbb{E}_{s,t}\Big[w_{s,t}\,\mathbb{E}\big[\|(\hat{X}_{s,t}(I_s) - \mathrm{ODESolve}_{t-\delta,t}(y_\delta))/\delta\|^2\big]\Big] \\
 &= \mathbb{E}_{s,t}\Big[w_{s,t}\,\mathbb{E}\big[\|(\hat{X}_{s,t}(I_s) - (y_\delta + \delta\, b_{t-\delta}(y_\delta)))/\delta + O(\delta)\|^2\big]\Big] \\
 &= \mathbb{E}_{s,t}\Big[w_{s,t}\,\mathbb{E}\big[\|(\hat{X}_{s,t}(I_s) - \hat{X}_{s,t-\delta}(I_s))/\delta - b_{t-\delta}(\hat{X}_{s,t-\delta}(I_s)) + O(\delta)\|^2\big]\Big] \\
 &\to \mathbb{E}_{s,t}\Big[w_{s,t}\,\mathbb{E}\big[\|\partial_t\hat{X}_{s,t}(I_s) - b_t(\hat{X}_{s,t}(I_s))\|^2\big]\Big] \quad \text{as } \delta \to 0 \\
 &= \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LMD}}(\hat{X}) .
\end{aligned}
$$
The third line is @eq-euler-step with $u = t-\delta$. In the limit, the
backward difference quotient converges to $\partial_t\hat{X}_{s,t}(I_s)$, and
$b_{t-\delta}(\hat{X}_{s,t-\delta}(I_s)) \to b_t(\hat{X}_{s,t}(I_s))$ by
continuity of $b$ and $\hat{X}$.
:::

The slide proves only the Lagrangian half. The Eulerian half is the one that
consistency models and CTM use, so we carry it out.

::: {#prp-eulerconv}
## Convergence of the discrete Eulerian loss
Under the assumptions above,
$\delta^{-2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DEMD}}(\hat{X}) \to \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{EMD}}(\hat{X})$
as $\delta \to 0$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Fix $(s,t)$ and $x = I_s$, and write
$x_\delta = \mathrm{ODESolve}_{s,s+\delta}(x) = x + \delta\, b_s(x) + O(\delta^2)$
by @eq-euler-step. Expand $\hat{X}_{s+\delta,t}(x_\delta)$ to first order
around $(s,x)$, in the start time and in the space variable simultaneously:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\hat{X}_{s+\delta,t}(x_\delta)
 &= \hat{X}_{s,t}(x) + \delta\,\partial_s\hat{X}_{s,t}(x) + \nabla\hat{X}_{s,t}(x)\,(x_\delta - x) + O(\delta^2) \\
 &= \hat{X}_{s,t}(x) + \delta\,\big[\partial_s\hat{X}_{s,t}(x) + \nabla\hat{X}_{s,t}(x)\, b_s(x)\big] + O(\delta^2) .
\end{aligned}
$$
Therefore
$$
\frac{\hat{X}_{s,t}(x) - \hat{X}_{s+\delta,t}(x_\delta)}{\delta}
 = -\big[\partial_s\hat{X}_{s,t}(x) + b_s(x)\cdot\nabla\hat{X}_{s,t}(x)\big] + O(\delta) .
$$ {#eq-demd-residual}
Taking the squared norm (the sign disappears), then the expectation over
$I_s$ and over $(s,t)$ with weight $w_{s,t}$, and letting $\delta\to0$ gives
$\delta^{-2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DEMD}}(\hat{X}) \to \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{EMD}}(\hat{X})$.
:::

@eq-demd-residual shows what the discrete Eulerian loss does: it is a finite
difference of the function $g(s) = \hat{X}_{s,t}(x_s)$ from the proof of
@prp-suff along a teacher trajectory. The loss asks that moving the starting
point a little along the teacher trajectory does not change where the student
lands. Both convergence statements are checked numerically in @sec-ch15-worked.

::: {.callout-note}
## A question from the class: what if the loss is not the MSE?
A student asked what happens when the squared norm in the discrete losses is
replaced by another loss, as in @eq-naive where $d$ may be LPIPS. The following
answer was not given in the lecture and is not from the slides. Let $d(u,v) \ge 0$ be a
three times continuously differentiable loss with $d(u,v) = 0$ if and only if
$u = v$. The *minimizer* does not change: the discrete Eulerian loss is still
non-negative, and it is zero exactly when
$\hat{X}_{s,t} = \hat{X}_{s+\delta,t}\circ\mathrm{ODESolve}_{s,s+\delta}$ on
the support of $I_s$, the same condition as for the squared norm. What changes is the
*limit*. Since $v \mapsto d(u,v)$ has a minimum at $v = u$, its first-order
term vanishes and $d(u, u + \delta r) = \tfrac{1}{2}\delta^2\, r^\top H(u)\, r + O(\delta^3)$
with $H(u) = \nabla_v^2 d(u,v)\vert_{v=u}$ positive semi-definite.
By @eq-demd-residual, $\delta^{-2}$ times the discrete Eulerian loss then
converges to the Eulerian residual measured in the local metric
$\tfrac12 H$ instead of the Euclidean one. For the squared norm, $H = 2\,\mathrm{Id}$ and
we recover @prp-eulerconv. So a different loss gives a re-weighted version of the
same continuous objective. For the pseudo-Huber loss
$d(u,v) = \sqrt{\|u-v\|^2 + c^2} - c$ used later in the lecture,
$H = \mathrm{Id}/c$, so the limit is the Eulerian loss itself divided by $2c$.
LPIPS, the other loss used by consistency models, is a distance between
network features and does not satisfy these hypotheses exactly (it is not
smooth, and it can vanish for $u \neq v$), so for it the statement is only a
heuristic.
:::

### Intuitive picture

The slides explain the two discrete losses with the same drawing, built up
step by step and reproduced in @fig-schematic. Start from a point $x_s$. The
green curve is the trajectory of the teacher's probability flow ODE (PF-ODE,
the ODE @eq-pfode) through $x_s$; it reaches
the correct answer $x_t$. The red curve is the *flow map trajectory*
$t \mapsto \hat{X}_{s,t}(x_s)$ of the current student, which starts at the same
point (boundary condition) and ends at the wrong place $\hat{X}_{s,t}(x_s)$.

* **LMD** (panel a). Stop the student slightly early, at
  $\hat{X}_{s,t-\delta}(x_s)$. From that point let the teacher advance for the
  remaining time $\delta$: this gives
  $\mathrm{ODESolve}_{t-\delta,t}(\hat{X}_{s,t-\delta}(x_s))$. Minimize the
  distance between this point and the student's own prediction
  $\hat{X}_{s,t}(x_s)$. The student is asked to extend its own trajectory in
  the direction the teacher prescribes: the *end* of the jump is perturbed.
* **EMD** (panel b). Let the teacher advance first, from $x_s$ to
  $\mathrm{ODESolve}_{s,s+\delta}(x_s)$, which lies on the green curve. From
  there let the student jump to time $t$:
  $\hat{X}_{s+\delta,t}(\mathrm{ODESolve}_{s,s+\delta}(x_s))$. Minimize the
  distance between this point and $\hat{X}_{s,t}(x_s)$. Two student jumps that
  start on the same teacher trajectory are asked to land at the same place:
  the *start* of the jump is perturbed.

![The discrete distillation losses, redrawn from the slides. Red: flow map
trajectories of the student. Green: PF-ODE trajectories of the teacher. (a)
Discrete LMD compares the student's jump to $t$ with its jump to $t-\delta$
followed by a teacher step. (b) Discrete EMD compares the student's jump from
$x_s$ with its jump from the point one teacher step later on the same
trajectory. (c) With a stop-gradient the second point is a fixed target and
only $\hat{X}_{s,t}(x_s)$ is moved; this is the loss of consistency models and
CTM.](figures/lec15/ChungEunho-distillation-schematic.png){#fig-schematic width=100%}

## Flow Map Training in Practice

The second part of the lecture reads the main few-step generators as flow map
training: consistency models, CTM, MeanFlow and flow map matching. This
lecture covered consistency models, latent consistency models and CTM;
MeanFlow and flow map matching belong to the next one.

### Timeline

The lecture opened this part with the history of the FID (Frechet inception
distance, a measure of sample quality; lower is better) on ImageNet
$256\times256$, redrawn in @fig-timeline from the numbers on the slide.
Many-step models improved steadily: ADM (1000 NFE, FID 4.59, 2021), DiT
($250\times2$ NFE, FID 2.27, 2023), REPA ($250\times2$ NFE, FID 1.42, 2025) and
RAE ($250\times2$ NFE, FID 1.13, 2026). One-step models started far behind,
with iCT at 34.24 FID for 1 NFE in 2024, and then closed almost the whole gap
in two years: MeanFlow (1 NFE, FID 3.43, 2025) and FreeFlow (1 NFE, FID 1.45,
2026). The slide labels this the *big leap from CM to flow map*.

![FID on ImageNet $256\times256$ over time, from the numbers on the lecture
slide (the vertical axis is logarithmic here). One-step generators (red) went
from 34.24 to 1.45 between 2024 and 2026 and are now close to many-step models
(blue) that use $250\times2$ network evaluations. The change of slope
coincides with the move from consistency models, which learn only jumps to the
endpoint, to general flow maps.](figures/lec15/ChungEunho-timeline.png){#fig-timeline width=75%}

Why did one-step generation improve so much once flow maps replaced
consistency models? The explanation given in the lecture is that a flow map
learns *all* transitions between two times, not only the transitions into the
endpoint, and that learning every transition $s \to t$ makes the particular
transition needed for one-step generation better. The CTM section makes this
concrete: the extra destination time connects the model to flow matching,
which grounds it in data.

### Consistency models {#sec-cm}

Consistency models (Song, Dhariwal, Chen and Sutskever, ICML 2023) were the
first widely used one-step model of this kind. The slide shows their samples
on ImageNet next to those of the teacher: the EDM teacher (the diffusion model
of Karras et al., see the references) reaches FID 2.44 with many steps and consistency distillation (CD) reaches FID 6.20 with
*single-step* generation, with visibly the same image content for the same
noise. In the present language a consistency model is a flow map with the
destination time frozen.

::: {#def-cm}
## Consistency model (slide Definition 3)
A *consistency model* $X_s : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d$ is the unique map
such that
$$
X_s(x_s) = X_{s,1}(x_s) = x_1 \qquad \forall s \in [0,1],
$$ {#eq-cm}
where $(x_t)_{t\in[0,1]}$ is any solution to the ODE $\dot{x}_t = b_t(x_t)$.
*Consistency distillation* minimizes
$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CD}}(\hat{X}) = \mathbb{E}_{s\in[0,1]}\Big[w_s\,\big\|\hat{X}_s(I_s) - \mathrm{sg}\big[\hat{X}_{s+\delta}(\mathrm{ODESolve}_{s,s+\delta}(I_s))\big]\big\|^2\Big]
$$ {#eq-cd}
subject to $\hat{X}_1(x) = x$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$.
:::

The *target point is fixed and the starting point is arbitrary*: every point
of a trajectory is mapped to the same endpoint $x_1$, which is the
"self-consistency" that gives the model its name. The figure on the slide
(from the paper) shows three points of one PF-ODE trajectory between data and
noise, all sent to the same data point by $f_\theta$.

Compare @eq-cd with the discrete Eulerian loss @eq-demd. Setting $t = 1$ in
@eq-demd and writing $\hat{X}_s = \hat{X}_{s,1}$ and $w_s = w_{s,1}$ gives
$$
\mathbb{E}_{s}\Big[w_s\,\mathbb{E}\big[\|\hat{X}_s(I_s) - \hat{X}_{s+\delta}(\mathrm{ODESolve}_{s,s+\delta}(I_s))\|^2\big]\Big],
$$
and the boundary condition $\hat{X}_{t,t} = \mathrm{id}$ at $t=1$ is
$\hat{X}_1(x) = x$. So consistency distillation is *very similar to discrete
Eulerian map distillation with $t = 1$, but with a stop-gradient*. Why the
stop-gradient?

**The role of the stop-gradient.** Without it, the loss @eq-demd is symmetric
in its two points: the gradient moves both $\hat{X}_{s,t}(x_s)$ and
$\hat{X}_{s+\delta,t}(\mathrm{ODESolve}_{s,s+\delta}(x_s))$, and the slide
describes this as *pulling the points towards each other*. But the two points
are not equally trustworthy. Take $s < t$, as in the pictures. The second one
starts one teacher step closer to the destination, where the boundary condition pins the model to the identity,
so it is the *more accurate* of the two. With the stop-gradient *the more
accurate point is fixed* and only the less accurate one is pulled toward it,
as in panel (c) of @fig-schematic. The loss becomes a regression onto a target
produced by the model itself, with information flowing in one direction, from
the boundary $s = t$ outward. This is the same direction in which the proof of
the Eulerian case of @prp-suff propagates the boundary condition.

The claim that the fixed point is still the right one can be made precise on
a time grid. The statement and proof are not on the slides.

::: {#prp-fixed}
## Fixed point of the stop-gradient loss
Let $s_k = k\delta$, $k = 0,\dots,K$, with $K\delta = 1$, and consider
@eq-cd with $s$ restricted to the grid, $w_{s_k} > 0$, and $\rho_{s_k} > 0$
everywhere. Suppose the model class can represent any function at each grid
time, and that the functions at different grid times are parametrized
independently of each other. Then the only $\hat{X}$ that is a fixed point of gradient descent
on @eq-cd, and satisfies $\hat{X}_{s_K} = \mathrm{id}$, is
$$
\hat{X}_{s_k} = \mathrm{ODESolve}_{s_{K-1},s_K} \circ \cdots \circ \mathrm{ODESolve}_{s_{k+1},s_{k+2}} \circ \mathrm{ODESolve}_{s_k,s_{k+1}},
$$
the teacher's own multi-step solution from $s_k$ to $1$.
:::

::: {.proof}
With the target held constant, the loss at grid time $s_k$ is an ordinary
least-squares regression of $\hat{X}_{s_k}(I_{s_k})$ onto the value
$T_k(I_{s_k})$, where $T_k = \hat{X}_{s_{k+1}}\circ\mathrm{ODESolve}_{s_k,s_{k+1}}$.
Its gradient with respect to the function $\hat{X}_{s_k}$ is
$2 w_{s_k}(\hat{X}_{s_k} - T_k)\rho_{s_k}$, which vanishes only if
$\hat{X}_{s_k} = T_k$ wherever $\rho_{s_k} > 0$, that is everywhere. So a
fixed point satisfies
$\hat{X}_{s_k} = \hat{X}_{s_{k+1}}\circ\mathrm{ODESolve}_{s_k,s_{k+1}}$ for
$k = 0,\dots,K-1$. Starting from $\hat{X}_{s_K} = \mathrm{id}$ and going
backward in $k$ gives the stated composition by induction.
:::

Two lessons follow. First, with the stop-gradient the only fixed point is the
teacher's discretized flow map, and the boundary condition is the only thing
that selects it. (The proposition is about fixed points of an idealized model
class; it does not prove that training a neural network converges to it.)
Second, the student is exactly as accurate as the teacher run with step
$\delta$: distillation inherits the teacher's discretization error. Both are
visible in the worked example of @sec-ch15-worked, where the distilled one-step map
agrees with the 16-step Euler teacher to three digits rather than with the
exact flow map.

**The two training algorithms.** The slide reproduces Algorithms 2 and 3 of
the paper. The paper uses the EDM convention, in which the noisy point is
$\mathbf{x}_t = \mathbf{x} + t\mathbf{z}$ for data $\mathbf{x}$, times are
discretized as $t_1 < t_2 < \dots < t_N$, and the model
$\mathbf{f}_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t, t)$ maps a point at noise level $t$ to the
data end of its trajectory. The dictionary to the notation of the lecture is:

| Paper (Song et al., 2023) | Lecture |
|---|---|
| noisier time $t_{n+1}$, cleaner time $t_n$ | $s$ and $s+\delta$ (one step closer to the destination) |
| $\mathbf{x}_{t_{n+1}} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}; t_{n+1}^2 \mathbf{I})$ | $I_s$ |
| $\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{\phi}_{t_n} = \mathbf{x}_{t_{n+1}} + (t_n - t_{n+1})\Phi(\mathbf{x}_{t_{n+1}}, t_{n+1}; \phi)$ | $\mathrm{ODESolve}_{s,s+\delta}(I_s)$, one step of the teacher $\phi$ |
| $\mathbf{f}_\theta(\mathbf{x}_{t_{n+1}}, t_{n+1})$ | $\hat{X}_s(I_s)$ |
| $\mathbf{f}_{\theta^-}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{\phi}_{t_n}, t_n)$ | $\mathrm{sg}[\hat{X}_{s+\delta}(\cdot)]$ |
| $\lambda(t_n)$, $d(\cdot,\cdot)$ | $w_s$, $\Vert\cdot\Vert^2$ |

*Algorithm 2, consistency distillation (CD).* Input: dataset $\mathcal{D}$,
initial parameter $\theta$, learning rate $\eta$, ODE solver
$\Phi(\cdot,\cdot;\phi)$ built on a pre-trained teacher $\phi$, metric $d$,
weight $\lambda$, rate $\mu$ of the exponential moving average (EMA). Set
$\theta^- \leftarrow \theta$ and repeat until convergence:

1. sample $\mathbf{x} \sim \mathcal{D}$ and $n \sim \mathcal{U}[1, N-1]$;
2. sample $\mathbf{x}_{t_{n+1}} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}; t_{n+1}^2\mathbf{I})$;
3. $\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{\phi}_{t_n} \leftarrow \mathbf{x}_{t_{n+1}} + (t_n - t_{n+1})\,\Phi(\mathbf{x}_{t_{n+1}}, t_{n+1}; \phi)$;
4. $\mathcal{L}(\theta,\theta^-;\phi) \leftarrow \lambda(t_n)\, d\big(\mathbf{f}_\theta(\mathbf{x}_{t_{n+1}}, t_{n+1}),\ \mathbf{f}_{\theta^-}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{\phi}_{t_n}, t_n)\big)$;
5. $\theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta\nabla_\theta\mathcal{L}(\theta,\theta^-;\phi)$;
6. $\theta^- \leftarrow \mathrm{stopgrad}(\mu\theta^- + (1-\mu)\theta)$.

The stop-gradient of @eq-cd appears as a second copy $\theta^-$ of the
parameters, an exponential moving average (EMA) of $\theta$ that receives no
gradient.

*Algorithm 3, consistency training (CT).* There is no teacher. Input: dataset
$\mathcal{D}$, $\theta$, $\eta$, step schedule $N(\cdot)$, EMA decay schedule
$\mu(\cdot)$, $d$, $\lambda$. Set $\theta^-\leftarrow\theta$, $k \leftarrow 0$
and repeat until convergence:

1. sample $\mathbf{x}\sim\mathcal{D}$ and $n \sim \mathcal{U}[1, N(k)-1]$;
2. sample $\mathbf{z}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I})$;
3. $\mathcal{L}(\theta,\theta^-) \leftarrow \lambda(t_n)\, d\big(\mathbf{f}_\theta(\mathbf{x} + t_{n+1}\mathbf{z}, t_{n+1}),\ \mathbf{f}_{\theta^-}(\mathbf{x} + t_n\mathbf{z}, t_n)\big)$;
4. $\theta\leftarrow\theta - \eta\nabla_\theta\mathcal{L}(\theta,\theta^-)$;
5. $\theta^-\leftarrow\mathrm{stopgrad}(\mu(k)\theta^- + (1-\mu(k))\theta)$;
6. $k \leftarrow k+1$.

The only difference in the loss is the second argument:
$\hat{\mathbf{x}}^\phi_{t_n}$ is replaced by $\mathbf{x} + t_n\mathbf{z}$ with
the *same* $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{z}$ that produced
$\mathbf{x}_{t_{n+1}}$. The slides do not say where this comes from; it is one
Euler step in which the teacher is replaced by a one-sample estimate.

::: {#prp-ct}
## Consistency training is distillation with a one-sample teacher
In the EDM convention the PF-ODE is
$d\mathbf{x}_t/dt = -t\,\nabla\log p_t(\mathbf{x}_t)$. Replace the score in
the Euler step of Algorithm 2 by its unbiased one-sample estimate given
$(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z})$. Then
$\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t_n} = \mathbf{x} + t_n\mathbf{z}$.
:::

::: {.proof}
For $\mathbf{x}_t = \mathbf{x} + t\mathbf{z}$ the score satisfies
$\nabla\log p_t(\mathbf{x}_t) = -\mathbb{E}[(\mathbf{x}_t - \mathbf{x})/t^2 \mid \mathbf{x}_t]$,
so $-(\mathbf{x}_t - \mathbf{x})/t^2 = -\mathbf{z}/t$ is an unbiased estimate
of it given $\mathbf{x}_t$. With this estimate the ODE drift is
$\Phi = -t\cdot(-\mathbf{z}/t) = \mathbf{z}$, and the Euler step from
$t_{n+1}$ to $t_n$ gives
$$
\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t_n} = \mathbf{x}_{t_{n+1}} + (t_n - t_{n+1})\,\mathbf{z}
 = \mathbf{x} + t_{n+1}\mathbf{z} + (t_n - t_{n+1})\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{x} + t_n\mathbf{z} .
$$
:::

This resembles @prp-learn, where the intractable $b_t(I_t)$ was replaced by
the sample $\dot{I}_t$, but there is an important difference. In
@prp-learn the noisy target enters the squared loss linearly, so the minimizer
is exactly unchanged. Here the one-sample velocity $\mathbf{z}$ is passed
through the nonlinear map $\mathbf{f}_{\theta^-}(\cdot, t_n)$ and then through
$d$, and an unbiased velocity does not give an unbiased target. The
replacement is justified only to leading order in the step: linearizing
$\mathbf{f}_{\theta^-}(\mathbf{x}_{t_{n+1}} + (t_n - t_{n+1})\mathbf{v}, t_n)$
in the step size makes the target linear in the velocity $\mathbf{v}$ up to
second-order terms, so the CT loss agrees with the CD loss up to an error that
vanishes faster than the step size (this is the content of Theorem 2 of Song
et al., 2023). The price of having no teacher is therefore a noisier target
and a bias that disappears only as the grid is refined. The comment made in
the lecture on this slide was that, in practice, *distillation is usually much
better* than training from scratch.

**Follow-up work.** The lecture listed the line of papers that made
consistency models competitive without a teacher, without going into them:
*Consistency Models* (ICML 2023), *Improved Techniques for Training
Consistency Models* (ICLR 2024, oral) and *Simplifying, Stabilizing and
Scaling Continuous-Time Consistency Models* (ICLR 2025, oral). The slide shows
Table 1 of the second paper, which compares its design choices for CT with the
original ones:

| Design choice | Song et al. (2023) | Improved techniques (iCT) |
|---|---|---|
| EMA decay rate for the teacher network | $\mu(k) = \exp\big(\frac{s_0\log\mu_0}{N(k)}\big)$ | $\mu(k) = 0$ |
| Metric in the consistency loss | $d(x,y) = \mathrm{LPIPS}(x,y)$ | $d(x,y) = \sqrt{\Vert x-y\Vert_2^2 + c^2} - c$ |
| Discretization curriculum | $N(k) = \big\lceil\sqrt{\tfrac{k}{K}((s_1+1)^2 - s_0^2) + s_0^2} - 1\big\rceil + 1$ | $N(k) = \min(s_0 2^{\lfloor k/K'\rfloor}, s_1) + 1$, $K' = \big\lfloor\frac{K}{\log_2\lfloor s_1/s_0\rfloor + 1}\big\rfloor$ |
| Noise schedule | $\sigma_i$ with $i\sim\mathcal{U}[1, N(k)-1]$ | $\sigma_i$ with $i \sim p(i)$, $p(i)\propto \mathrm{erf}\big(\frac{\log\sigma_{i+1} - P_{\mathrm{mean}}}{\sqrt2 P_{\mathrm{std}}}\big) - \mathrm{erf}\big(\frac{\log\sigma_i - P_{\mathrm{mean}}}{\sqrt2 P_{\mathrm{std}}}\big)$ |
| Weighting function | $\lambda(\sigma_i) = 1$ | $\lambda(\sigma_i) = \frac{1}{\sigma_{i+1} - \sigma_i}$ |
| Parameters | $s_0 = 2$, $s_1 = 150$, $\mu_0 = 0.9$ on CIFAR-10; $s_0 = 2$, $s_1 = 200$, $\mu_0 = 0.95$ on ImageNet $64\times64$ | $s_0 = 10$, $s_1 = 1280$, $c = 0.00054\sqrt{d}$ ($d$ the data dimension), $P_{\mathrm{mean}} = -1.1$, $P_{\mathrm{std}} = 2.0$ |

In both columns $k \in [0,K]$ is the training iteration, $K$ the total number
of iterations, and
$\sigma_i = \big(\sigma_{\min}^{1/\rho} + \frac{i-1}{N(k)-1}(\sigma_{\max}^{1/\rho} - \sigma_{\min}^{1/\rho})\big)^{\rho}$
for $i \in [1, N(k)]$ with $\rho = 7$, $\sigma_{\min} = 0.002$,
$\sigma_{\max} = 80$. The
following reading of the table through the flow map picture is an
interpretation; it was not discussed in the lecture. $\mu(k) = 0$ means $\theta^- = \theta$,
that is a pure stop-gradient with no EMA, exactly the $\mathrm{sg}$
of @eq-cd. The number of grid points $N(k)$ grows during training, so the step
$\delta$ shrinks and the fixed point of the loss, the teacher's discretized
solution (@prp-fixed), approaches the true flow map. The weight
$1/(\sigma_{i+1}-\sigma_i)$ is $1/\delta$ measured in noise levels. This is
the natural normalization for a loss with a stop-gradient: its gradient is
$2(\hat{X}_s - \mathrm{sg}[\cdot])^\top\nabla_\theta\hat{X}_s$, which is of
order $\delta$ by @eq-demd-residual, so dividing by $\delta$ keeps the update
of order one as the grid is refined (without the stop-gradient one would
divide the loss by $\delta^2$, as in @prp-eulerconv). The paper's own
motivation for this weight is that it puts more emphasis on small noise
levels, where the non-uniform grid is finest. Finally, the pseudo-Huber
metric replaces LPIPS; by the remark after @prp-eulerconv it rescales the
Eulerian residual without changing where it vanishes.

### Latent consistency models

Latent consistency models (Luo, Tan, Huang, Li and Zhao, arXiv:2310.04378)
apply consistency distillation to a pre-trained text-to-image latent diffusion
model. The lecture went through these slides quickly. The headline, from the
figure caption on the slide: LCMs can be distilled from any pre-trained Stable
Diffusion model in only 4,000 training steps (about 32 A100 GPU hours) and
generate $768\times768$ images in 2 to 4 steps or even one step. The samples
on the slide at 4 steps and 2 steps are sharp; the 1-step sample is visibly
blurrier.

Three ingredients are added to consistency distillation, corresponding to the
four formulas on the slide. Here $\mathbf{z}_t$ is a *latent* code (the image
encoded by the autoencoder of the latent diffusion model, not the Gaussian
variable $z$ of @def-interpolant), $\mathbf{c}$ is the text condition,
$\varnothing$ the empty condition, $\omega$ the guidance scale, and
$\alpha_t,\sigma_t$ the signal and noise scales of the diffusion model.

1. **Classifier-free guidance is part of the teacher.** The guided noise
   prediction is
$$
\tilde{\boldsymbol\epsilon}_\theta(\mathbf{z}_t,\omega,\mathbf{c},t) := (1+\omega)\,\boldsymbol\epsilon_\theta(\mathbf{z}_t,\mathbf{c},t) - \omega\,\boldsymbol\epsilon_\theta(\mathbf{z}_t,\varnothing,t),
$$
   and the ODE that is distilled is the *augmented* PF-ODE
$$
\frac{d\mathbf{z}_t}{dt} = f(t)\,\mathbf{z}_t + \frac{g^2(t)}{2\sigma_t}\,\tilde{\boldsymbol\epsilon}_\theta(\mathbf{z}_t,\omega,\mathbf{c},t), \qquad \mathbf{z}_T\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\tilde\sigma^2\mathbf{I}) .
$$
   In the language of this lecture, the velocity $b$ whose flow map is learned
   is the guided velocity, so the student needs one evaluation where guided
   sampling needs two.
2. **The boundary condition is built in.** The consistency function is
   parametrized on top of the noise prediction network
   $\hat{\boldsymbol\epsilon}_\theta$ of the diffusion model as
$$
\mathbf{f}_\theta(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{c},t) = c_{\mathrm{skip}}(t)\,\mathbf{z} + c_{\mathrm{out}}(t)\Big(\frac{\mathbf{z} - \sigma_t\hat{\boldsymbol\epsilon}_\theta(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{c},t)}{\alpha_t}\Big) \qquad (\boldsymbol\epsilon\text{-prediction}),
$$
   where $c_{\mathrm{skip}}$ and $c_{\mathrm{out}}$ are chosen so that
   $c_{\mathrm{skip}} = 1$ and $c_{\mathrm{out}} = 0$ at the data end. This
   is the constraint $\hat{X}_1(x) = x$ of @def-cm. The term in parentheses
   is the data prediction implied by $\hat{\boldsymbol\epsilon}_\theta$, so
   the pre-trained network can be reused as initialization.
3. **The guidance scale is an input.** The loss is the CD loss with $\omega$
   sampled and fed to the model:
$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{CD}}(\theta,\theta^-;\Psi) = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z},\mathbf{c},\omega,n}\Big[d\big(\mathbf{f}_\theta(\mathbf{z}_{t_{n+1}},\omega,\mathbf{c},t_{n+1}),\ \mathbf{f}_{\theta^-}(\hat{\mathbf{z}}^{\Psi,\omega}_{t_n},\omega,\mathbf{c},t_n)\big)\Big].
$$

*Algorithm 1, latent consistency distillation (LCD)*, as on the slide. Input:
dataset $\mathcal{D}$, $\theta$, $\eta$, ODE solver $\Psi(\cdot,\cdot,\cdot,\cdot)$,
metric $d$, EMA rate $\mu$, noise schedule $\alpha(t),\sigma(t)$, guidance
scale range $[\omega_{\min},\omega_{\max}]$, skipping interval $k$, encoder
$E$. Encode the data into latent space,
$\mathcal{D}_z = \{(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{c}) \mid \mathbf{z} = E(\mathbf{x}),\ (\mathbf{x},\mathbf{c})\in\mathcal{D}\}$,
set $\theta^-\leftarrow\theta$ and repeat until convergence:

1. sample $(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{c})\sim\mathcal{D}_z$, $n\sim\mathcal{U}[1, N-k]$ and $\omega\sim[\omega_{\min},\omega_{\max}]$;
2. sample $\mathbf{z}_{t_{n+k}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\alpha(t_{n+k})\mathbf{z};\ \sigma^2(t_{n+k})\mathbf{I})$;
3. $\hat{\mathbf{z}}^{\Psi,\omega}_{t_n}\leftarrow\mathbf{z}_{t_{n+k}} + (1+\omega)\Psi(\mathbf{z}_{t_{n+k}}, t_{n+k}, t_n, \mathbf{c}) - \omega\Psi(\mathbf{z}_{t_{n+k}}, t_{n+k}, t_n, \varnothing)$;
4. $\mathcal{L}(\theta,\theta^-;\Psi)\leftarrow d\big(\mathbf{f}_\theta(\mathbf{z}_{t_{n+k}},\omega,\mathbf{c},t_{n+k}),\ \mathbf{f}_{\theta^-}(\hat{\mathbf{z}}^{\Psi,\omega}_{t_n},\omega,\mathbf{c},t_n)\big)$;
5. $\theta\leftarrow\theta-\eta\nabla_\theta\mathcal{L}(\theta,\theta^-)$;
6. $\theta^-\leftarrow\mathrm{stopgrad}(\mu\theta^- + (1-\mu)\theta)$.

The loss formula above is written for adjacent grid points, $t_{n+1}\to t_n$,
while the algorithm uses $t_{n+k}\to t_n$; the formula is the case $k = 1$.
Compared with Algorithm 2 of consistency models, step 3 is the teacher step
with guidance, and the *skipping interval* $k$ means that the teacher step jumps $k$ grid points
at once ($t_{n+k}\to t_n$). In the notation of @eq-cd this is a larger
$\delta$. A plausible reading (not from the lecture) is that each update then
propagates the boundary information further, which helps explain why so few
training steps suffice, at the price of a larger discretization error in the
target (@prp-fixed).

### Consistency trajectory models {#sec-ctm}

A consistency model can only jump to the endpoint. Consistency trajectory
models (Kim, Lai, Liao, Murata, Takida, Uesaka, He, Mitsufuji and Ermon, ICLR
2024) learn jumps between arbitrary times, that is, the full flow map.

The slide motivates this with Figure 1 of the paper, which compares three
families in training and in sampling:

* *Score-based models* estimate the score, a local quantity. With NFE $= 1$
  the single large solver step has a large discretization error; with more
  steps the error shrinks but never vanishes.
* *Distillation models* (such as consistency models) estimate the endpoint of
  the PF-ODE. NFE $= 1$ works. With NFE $> 1$ they must alternate "jump to the
  data end" and "add noise back", and the errors of the repeated long jumps
  accumulate.
* *CTM* estimates the entire PF-ODE trajectory, so it can jump to the endpoint
  in one step or move along the trajectory in several short jumps without
  re-noising.

::: {#def-ctm}
## Consistency trajectory model (slide Definition 4)
A *consistency trajectory model* is the unique map $X_{s,t}$ such that
$$
X_{s,t}(x_s) = x_t \qquad \forall s,t\in[0,1]^2,
$$
where $(x_t)_{t\in[0,1]}$ is any solution to the ODE $\dot{x}_t = b_t(x_t)$.
*CTM* minimizes
$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CTM}}(\hat{X}) = \mathbb{E}_{s,t\in[0,1]}\Big[w_{s,t}\,\big\|\hat{X}_{s,t}(I_s) - \mathrm{sg}\big[\hat{X}_{s+\delta,t}(\mathrm{ODESolve}_{s,s+\delta}(I_s))\big]\big\|^2\Big]
$$ {#eq-ctm}
subject to $\hat{X}_{s,s}(x) = x$ for all $x\in\mathbb{R}^d$.
:::

(The slide prints the map as "$X_s$" and the defining identity as
"$X_{s,t}(x_s) = X_{s,t}(x_s) = x_t$"; these are carried over from the
consistency model slide, and the definition above is the intended one.) The
object in @def-ctm is exactly the flow map of @def-flowmap, and the loss
is *very similar to discrete Eulerian map distillation, but with a
stop-gradient*: @eq-ctm is @eq-demd with the second point held fixed. For
$t = 1$ it reduces to consistency distillation @eq-cd. The analysis of
@sec-cm carries over with a general $t$.

**The connection to flow matching.** CTM *revealed an interesting connection
between flow maps and flow matching*. Suppose we use the parametrization
$$
X_{s,t}(x) = x + (t-s)\,F_{s,t}(x) .
$$ {#eq-param}
It satisfies the boundary condition $X_{s,s}(x) = x$ automatically. To see
what $F$ is, integrate the ODE along a trajectory from $s$ to $t$:
$$
X_{s,t}(x_s) = x_s + (t-s)F_{s,t}(x_s) = x_s + \int_s^t b_\tau(x_\tau)\,d\tau ,
$$
so
$$
F_{s,t}(x_s) = \frac{1}{t-s}\int_s^t b_\tau(x_\tau)\,d\tau
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
F_{s,s}(x_s) = b_s(x_s) .
$$ {#eq-avgvel}
The displacement $(t-s)F_{s,t}$ represents the integral of the velocity field
along the trajectory, and $F_{s,t}$ itself is that integral normalized by the
elapsed time: the *average velocity* over $[s,t]$. Letting $t\to s$, the
average of a continuous function over a shrinking interval tends to its value
at $s$, which gives $F_{s,s} = b_s$. On its diagonal, a flow map in this
parametrization *is* the velocity field.

The slide then leaves an exercise: in fact, $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{EMD}}$
becomes flow matching in the limit $t = s$. Here is the solution.

::: {#prp-fm-limit}
## The Eulerian loss on the diagonal is flow matching (slide exercise)
Let $\hat{X}_{s,t}(x) = x + (t-s)\hat{F}_{s,t}(x)$ with $\hat{F}$ continuously
differentiable. Then the Eulerian residual is
$$
\partial_s\hat{X}_{s,t}(x) + b_s(x)\cdot\nabla\hat{X}_{s,t}(x)
 = \big(b_s(x) - \hat{F}_{s,t}(x)\big) + (t-s)\big(\partial_s\hat{F}_{s,t}(x) + b_s(x)\cdot\nabla\hat{F}_{s,t}(x)\big),
$$ {#eq-residual-F}
and in the limit $t\to s$ the integrand of $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{EMD}}$ becomes
$$
w_{s,s}\,\mathbb{E}\big[\|\hat{F}_{s,s}(I_s) - b_s(I_s)\|^2\big]
 = w_{s,s}\Big(\mathbb{E}\big[\|\hat{F}_{s,s}(I_s) - \dot{I}_s\|^2\big] - \mathbb{E}\big[\|b_s(I_s) - \dot{I}_s\|^2\big]\Big),
$$ {#eq-fm-limit}
which is the flow matching regression @eq-regression for the velocity model
$\hat{b}_s = \hat{F}_{s,s}$, up to a constant that does not depend on
$\hat{F}$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Differentiate the parametrization. In $s$, the product rule gives
$\partial_s\hat{X}_{s,t}(x) = -\hat{F}_{s,t}(x) + (t-s)\,\partial_s\hat{F}_{s,t}(x)$.
In $x$, $\nabla\hat{X}_{s,t}(x) = \mathrm{Id} + (t-s)\nabla\hat{F}_{s,t}(x)$ (with $\mathrm{Id}$ the identity matrix), hence
$b_s(x)\cdot\nabla\hat{X}_{s,t}(x) = b_s(x) + (t-s)\,b_s(x)\cdot\nabla\hat{F}_{s,t}(x)$.
Adding the two gives @eq-residual-F. At $t = s$ the second bracket is
multiplied by zero and the residual is $b_s(x) - \hat{F}_{s,s}(x)$; inserting
it into @eq-emd gives the left-hand side of @eq-fm-limit. The right-hand side
is the decomposition @eq-decomp from the proof of @prp-learn applied to
$\hat{b}_s = \hat{F}_{s,s}$.
:::

Two things are worth noticing. The limit loss can be evaluated *without the
teacher*: by @eq-fm-limit, regressing $\hat{F}_{s,s}(I_s)$ on the sample
$\dot{I}_s$ has the same minimizer. And @eq-residual-F shows the structure of
the whole Eulerian loss in this parametrization: a flow matching error plus
$(t-s)$ times a transport term for the average velocity.

**Stabilizing training.** *This connection plays a great role in stabilizing
flow map training.* Observe that the CTM loss @eq-ctm is a *bootstrapping*
type of loss, where the target also moves: the regression target
$\mathrm{sg}[\hat{X}_{s+\delta,t}(\cdot)]$ is produced by the network that is
being trained. Nothing in the loss itself refers to data; the correct solution
is selected only by the boundary condition, from which information has to
propagate step by step (@prp-fixed). As a result *there is a tendency for flow
maps to collapse to a constant function*. The slide only states this
tendency. One way to see why it is possible (an interpretation, not from the lecture) is
that the two sides of @eq-ctm agree whenever the model's output hardly
depends on its input, in the same way that a constant has zero Eulerian
residual; only the boundary condition rules such solutions out, and it acts
on the loss only indirectly. With the
parametrization $\hat{X}_{s,t}(x) = x + (t-s)F_{s,t}(x)$, adding the flow
matching loss
$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}(\hat{X}) = \mathbb{E}_{s\in[0,1]}\big[w_s\,\|F_{s,s}(I_s) - b_s(I_s)\|^2\big]
$$ {#eq-lfm}
*provides a stable target which grounds the model to data*. By
@prp-fm-limit this is not an unrelated regularizer but the diagonal part of
the Eulerian loss itself, and its target is not bootstrapped: it is the fixed
velocity $b_s$, or its data sample $\dot{I}_s$.

**Significance of this work.** The lecture summarized CTM in three points.

1. *Introduction of a secondary, "destination time" parameter $t$ to CMs.*
   The model is a function of $(x, s, t)$ and not only of $(x,s)$.
2. *Connection to flow matching, and thus stabler training*, as just shown.
3. *Enabled multi-step sampling*, for example
$$
x_1 = (X_{t_2,1}\circ X_{t_1,t_2}\circ X_{0,t_1})(x_0), \qquad 0 < t_1 < t_2 < 1 ,
$$ {#eq-multistep}
   which for the exact flow map equals $X_{0,1}(x_0)$ by the composition
   property (@prp-ch15-semigroup). For a learned flow map the two differ, and
   three short jumps are usually more accurate than one long jump.

The plot on the slide shows FID against NFE for the samplers of the paper.
The paper calls its family $\gamma$-*sampling*. In the paper's convention
(noise level $t$, data at $t = 0$), a step from the current noise level to the
next grid level $t_{n+1}$ is made in two parts: the model jumps *past*
$t_{n+1}$, down to the lower noise level $\sqrt{1-\gamma^2}\,t_{n+1}$, and
then Gaussian noise of scale $\gamma\,t_{n+1}$ is added to come back up to
$t_{n+1}$. The parameter $\gamma\in[0,1]$ controls how much noise is
re-injected. $\gamma = 1$ is the multistep sampler of consistency models
(jump all the way to the data end, then re-noise), and $\gamma = 0$ is the
deterministic composition @eq-multistep. On the slide, the three
$\gamma$-curves start together at an FID of about 5 for NFE 1 and improve to
about 4 within the first few steps. After that $\gamma = 1$ gets *worse* with
more steps, rising to above 10 at NFE 35, which is the error accumulation of
the repeated long jumps; $\gamma = 0.9$ degrades more slowly, to between 5 and
6; and $\gamma = 0$ keeps improving, to a little above 2. The fourth curve is
a classical second-order ODE solver (Heun) applied to the same network: it is
far worse at small NFE, crosses below FID 4 at about NFE 20, and meets the
$\gamma = 0$ curve only at about NFE 25.

**The loss used in the paper.** The full training objective of CTM, boxed on
the slide, has three terms:
$$
\mathcal{L}(\theta,\eta) := \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CTM}}(\theta;\phi) + \lambda_{\mathrm{DSM}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DSM}}(\theta) + \lambda_{\mathrm{GAN}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GAN}}(\theta,\eta),
$$
$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DSM}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{t,\mathbf{x}_0}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}_t\mid\mathbf{x}_0}\big[\|\mathbf{x}_0 - g_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t,t,t)\|_2^2\big],
$$
$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GAN}}(\theta,\eta) = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}_0}\big[\log d_\eta(\mathbf{x}_0)\big] + \mathbb{E}_{t\in[0,T]}\mathbb{E}_{s\in[0,t]}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}_0}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}_t\mid\mathbf{x}_0}\big[\log\big(1 - d_\eta(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{est}}(\mathbf{x}_t,t,s))\big)\big].
$$
The paper writes time the other way round from the lecture: $\mathbf{x}_0$ is
data, $t\in[0,T]$ is the noise level, and the model jumps from time $t$ to an
earlier time $s \le t$. Here $\phi$ is the teacher, $g_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t,t,s)$
is the network of the paper's parametrization of the jump from $t$ to $s$,
$d_\eta$ is a discriminator with parameters $\eta$, and
$\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{est}}(\mathbf{x}_t,t,s)$ is the model's estimate of the
clean sample obtained through the jump from $t$ to $s$. The three terms map
onto this lecture as follows.

* $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CTM}}$ is @eq-ctm. Figure 3 of the paper, on the
  slide, shows its two sides as *CTM's two predictions at time $s$ with an
  initial value $\mathbf{x}_t$*: a direct jump $t\to s$, and a teacher ODE
  solve $t\to u$ followed by a jump $u\to s$. This is panel (c)
  of @fig-schematic, with a multi-step solver in place of the single step
  $s\to s+\delta$.
* $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DSM}}$ (denoising score matching) evaluates the
  network on the diagonal, $g_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t,t,t)$, and regresses it on
  data. It is the counterpart of $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}$ in @eq-lfm: the
  diagonal of the flow map is a denoiser (equivalently a velocity) and is
  trained with a non-bootstrapped target.
* $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GAN}}$ is an adversarial loss on the model's outputs.
  It is not part of the flow map theory; it sharpens samples and allows the
  student to exceed the teacher.

The last slide shows Figure 4 of the paper (AFHQ-cat, $256\times256$), which
summarizes the section in one image. With score-based sampling, both EDM and
CTM give a sharp cat at NFE 40, an artifact-ridden one at NFE 4 and a blurry
average at NFE 1. With distillation sampling, CM and CTM give a sharp sample
already at NFE 1; for CTM the NFE-1 sample is the same for every $\gamma$
(the figure draws it once, with arrows to the other columns), since a single
jump involves no re-noising. At larger NFE, the samples of CM and of CTM with
$\gamma = 1$ and $\gamma = 0.5$ change identity from one NFE to the next,
because of the re-noising, while CTM with $\gamma = 0$ keeps the same cat and
only refines it.

## Worked Example {#sec-ch15-worked}

We carry one example through every object of the lecture, in closed form and
with code. Take $d = 1$,
$$
x_0\sim p_0 = \mathcal{N}(0, 1), \qquad x_1\sim p_1 = \mathcal{N}(2, 0.25),
$$
drawn independently, and the flow model interpolant $I_t = (1-t)x_0 + t x_1$.

**The velocity.** $I_t$ is Gaussian with mean $m_t = 2t$ and variance
$\sigma_t^2 = (1-t)^2 + 0.25\,t^2$. (In this section only, $\sigma_t$ denotes
the standard deviation of $I_t$; it is unrelated to the noise scales
$\sigma_t$ and $\sigma_i$ of the previous section.) The pair $(\dot{I}_t, I_t)$ with
$\dot{I}_t = x_1 - x_0$ is jointly Gaussian, with $\mathbb{E}[\dot{I}_t] = 2$
and
$$
\mathrm{Cov}(\dot{I}_t, I_t) = \mathrm{Cov}\big(x_1 - x_0,\ (1-t)x_0 + t x_1\big) = 0.25\,t - (1-t) = \tfrac12\tfrac{d}{dt}\sigma_t^2 = \sigma_t\dot\sigma_t .
$$
The conditional mean of a jointly Gaussian pair is linear, so by @eq-velocity
$$
b_t(x) = \mathbb{E}[\dot{I}_t\mid I_t = x] = 2 + \frac{\mathrm{Cov}(\dot{I}_t, I_t)}{\sigma_t^2}(x - m_t) = 2 + \frac{\dot\sigma_t}{\sigma_t}\,(x - 2t) .
$$

**The flow map.** The ODE $\dot{x}_t = 2 + (\dot\sigma_t/\sigma_t)(x_t - 2t)$
is linear. With $u_t = x_t - 2t$ it reads $\dot{u}_t = (\dot\sigma_t/\sigma_t)u_t$,
so $u_t/\sigma_t$ is constant along trajectories and
$$
X_{s,t}(x) = 2t + \frac{\sigma_t}{\sigma_s}\,(x - 2s) .
$$ {#eq-ex-flowmap}
In particular $X_{0,1}(x) = 2 + 0.5\,x$, which indeed maps
$\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ to $\mathcal{N}(2, 0.25)$, as @prp-ch15-semigroup requires. One
can check the two equations of @prp-suff by hand:
$\partial_t X_{s,t}(x) = 2 + (\dot\sigma_t/\sigma_s)(x-2s) = b_t(X_{s,t}(x))$,
and
$\partial_s X_{s,t}(x) + b_s(x)\,\partial_x X_{s,t}(x) = -\tfrac{\sigma_t\dot\sigma_s}{\sigma_s^2}(x-2s) - \tfrac{2\sigma_t}{\sigma_s} + \tfrac{\sigma_t}{\sigma_s}\big(2 + \tfrac{\dot\sigma_s}{\sigma_s}(x-2s)\big) = 0$.
The average velocity of @eq-avgvel is
$F_{s,t}(x) = (X_{s,t}(x) - x)/(t-s)$, and one verifies $F_{s,t}(x)\to b_s(x)$
as $t\to s$.

**One Euler step collapses.** At $t = 0$, $\sigma_0 = 1$ and
$\dot\sigma_0 = -1$, so $b_0(x) = 2 - x$. A one-step Euler sampler therefore
outputs $x + b_0(x) = 2$ for *every* input: all samples collapse onto the mean
of $p_1$. This is general for independent endpoints,
$b_0(x) = \mathbb{E}[x_1 - x_0\mid x_0 = x] = \mathbb{E}[x_1] - x$, and it is
the one-dimensional version of the blurry NFE-1 images of score-based
sampling in the CTM figure. A one-step *flow map* does not have this problem.

**Code.** The script below (i) checks the Lagrangian and Eulerian equations
for @eq-ex-flowmap by finite differences, (ii) samples with $K$ Euler steps
of the teacher, (iii) distills a consistency model on a grid with the
stop-gradient loss @eq-cd, and (iv) checks the convergence of the discrete
losses (@cor-discrete, @prp-eulerconv) for a deliberately wrong map. It needs only
NumPy and runs in a few seconds.

```{.python}
import numpy as np

# Interpolant I_t = (1 - t) x0 + t x1 with x0 ~ N(m0, v0), x1 ~ N(m1, v1) independent.
m0, v0, m1, v1 = 0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 0.25

def mu(t):    return (1 - t) * m0 + t * m1
def sig(t):   return np.sqrt((1 - t) ** 2 * v0 + t ** 2 * v1)
def dsig(t):  return (t * v1 - (1 - t) * v0) / sig(t)

def b(t, x):                      # velocity b_t(x) = E[x1 - x0 | I_t = x]
    return (m1 - m0) + dsig(t) / sig(t) * (x - mu(t))

def X(s, t, x):                   # exact flow map X_{s,t}(x)
    return mu(t) + sig(t) / sig(s) * (x - mu(s))

def sample_I(s, n, rng):          # n samples of I_s (s may be an array of length n)
    return (1 - s) * rng.normal(m0, np.sqrt(v0), n) + s * rng.normal(m1, np.sqrt(v1), n)

# (i) Lagrangian and Eulerian equations, by central finite differences.
s, t, x, h = 0.3, 0.8, -0.7, 1e-5
dt_X = (X(s, t + h, x) - X(s, t - h, x)) / (2 * h)
ds_X = (X(s + h, t, x) - X(s - h, t, x)) / (2 * h)
dx_X = (X(s, t, x + h) - X(s, t, x - h)) / (2 * h)
print("X_{0.3,0.8}(-0.7)   =", round(X(s, t, x), 6))
print("Lagrangian residual =", abs(dt_X - b(t, X(s, t, x))))
print("Eulerian residual   =", abs(ds_X + b(s, x) * dx_X))

# (ii) Sampling with the teacher: K Euler steps from t = 0 to t = 1.
def euler(x, K):
    for k in range(K):
        x = x + b(k / K, x) / K
    return x

x0 = np.array([-1.0, 0.0, 1.0])
print("exact X_{0,1}       =", X(0.0, 1.0, x0))
for K in (1, 2, 4, 16, 64):
    print(f"Euler, K = {K:2d}       =", np.round(euler(x0, K), 4))

# (iii) Consistency distillation: X_hat_k(x) = A[k] + B[k] x approximates X_{s_k,1}
#       on the grid s_k = k / K, with the boundary condition X_hat_K(x) = x.
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
K, lr, batch = 16, 0.05, 256
A, B = np.zeros(K + 1), np.ones(K + 1)
for it in range(40000):
    k = rng.integers(0, K)                       # s = s_k, delta = 1 / K
    Is = sample_I(k / K, batch, rng)
    y = Is + b(k / K, Is) / K                    # ODESolve_{s,s+delta}(I_s): one Euler step
    target = A[k + 1] + B[k + 1] * y             # sg[...]: treated as a constant
    r = A[k] + B[k] * Is - target
    A[k] -= lr * 2 * r.mean()                    # gradient of mean(r^2) w.r.t. A[k]
    B[k] -= lr * 2 * (r * Is).mean()             # gradient of mean(r^2) w.r.t. B[k]
print("distilled one-step map: x -> %.4f + %.4f x" % (A[0], B[0]))
print("16-step Euler teacher : x -> %.4f + %.4f x"
      % (euler(0.0, 16), euler(1.0, 16) - euler(0.0, 16)))
print("exact flow map        : x -> %.4f + %.4f x"
      % (X(0, 1, 0.0), X(0, 1, 1.0) - X(0, 1, 0.0)))

# (iv) Discrete losses for a wrong map X_hat = X + 0.5 (t - s) sin(x), which
#      satisfies X_hat_{s,s} = id. The teacher step is one Euler step.
def Xh(s, t, x): return X(s, t, x) + 0.5 * (t - s) * np.sin(x)
n = 400000
s = rng.uniform(0.05, 0.70, n); t = rng.uniform(0.75, 0.95, n); Is = sample_I(s, n, rng)
emd = (Xh(s + h, t, Is) - Xh(s - h, t, Is)) / (2 * h) \
      + b(s, Is) * (Xh(s, t, Is + h) - Xh(s, t, Is - h)) / (2 * h)
lmd = (Xh(s, t + h, Is) - Xh(s, t - h, Is)) / (2 * h) - b(t, Xh(s, t, Is))
print("L_EMD = %.4f   L_LMD = %.4f" % (np.mean(emd ** 2), np.mean(lmd ** 2)))
for d in (0.2, 0.1, 0.05, 0.0125, 0.003125):
    demd = Xh(s, t, Is) - Xh(s + d, t, Is + d * b(s, Is))
    y = Xh(s, t - d, Is)
    dlmd = Xh(s, t, Is) - (y + d * b(t - d, y))
    print("delta = %.6f   DEMD/delta^2 = %.4f   DLMD/delta^2 = %.4f"
          % (d, np.mean(demd ** 2) / d ** 2, np.mean(dlmd ** 2) / d ** 2))
```

**Output and reading.** The script prints (values rounded):

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| $X_{0.3,0.8}(-0.7)$ | $0.787896$ |
| Lagrangian residual, Eulerian residual | about $10^{-11}$, $10^{-10}$ (finite-difference error) |
| exact $X_{0,1}$ at $x_0 = -1, 0, 1$ | $1.5,\ 2.0,\ 2.5$ |
| Euler, $K=1$ | $2.0,\ 2.0,\ 2.0$ |
| Euler, $K=2$ | $1.8,\ 2.0,\ 2.2$ |
| Euler, $K=4$ | $1.6595,\ 2.0,\ 2.3405$ |
| Euler, $K=16$ | $1.5443,\ 2.0,\ 2.4557$ |
| Euler, $K=64$ | $1.5114,\ 2.0,\ 2.4886$ |
| distilled one-step map | $x\mapsto 2.000 + 0.456\,x$ |
| 16-step Euler teacher | $x\mapsto 2.000 + 0.4557\,x$ |
| exact flow map | $x\mapsto 2.000 + 0.5000\,x$ |
| $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{EMD}}$, $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LMD}}$ of the wrong map | $0.281$, $0.103$ |
| $\delta^{-2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DEMD}}$ at $\delta = 0.2,\ 0.1,\ 0.05,\ 0.0125,\ 0.003125$ | $0.297,\ 0.282,\ 0.280,\ 0.280,\ 0.280$ |
| $\delta^{-2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DLMD}}$ at the same $\delta$ | $0.369,\ 0.232,\ 0.162,\ 0.116,\ 0.106$ |

The last digits of the stochastic entries (the distilled map and the losses
of the wrong map) are Monte Carlo estimates: they depend on the random seed
and on the NumPy version in the third digit (the right panel of @fig-worked
was computed with a different seed). The
conclusions are:

* The closed-form flow map satisfies both equations of @prp-suff.
* The Euler sampler needs many steps: one step collapses to the mean, and
  even 16 steps give a slope of $0.456$ instead of $0.5$ (the samples are too
  concentrated). The teacher's error decays only like $1/K$.
* The distilled student reproduces in **one** evaluation what the teacher does
  in 16, and it matches the 16-step teacher, not the exact flow map, exactly
  as @prp-fixed predicts. A one-step student is cheap, but it cannot be more
  faithful to the true distribution than the teacher steps it was trained on,
  unless something else (a finer $\delta$, or the extra losses of CTM) is
  added.
* $\delta^{-2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DEMD}}\to\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{EMD}}$ and
  $\delta^{-2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DLMD}}\to\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LMD}}$ as
  $\delta\to0$, with an error of order $\delta$, as in
  @cor-discrete and @prp-eulerconv.

## Summary

* A stochastic interpolant $I_t = \alpha_t x_0 + \beta_t x_1 + \gamma_t z$
  covers flow models and diffusion models. Its marginals are transported by
  the ODE $\dot{x}_t = b_t(x_t)$ with $b_t(x) = \mathbb{E}[\dot{I}_t\mid I_t = x]$,
  and $b$ is learned by regression on $\dot{I}_t$.
* The flow map $X_{s,t}$ is the solution operator of that ODE. Learning it
  from its definition requires full ODE solves; its first-order
  characterizations do not.
* $X$ is a flow map if and only if it satisfies the Lagrangian equation
  $\partial_t X_{s,t} = b_t(X_{s,t})$ or the Eulerian equation
  $\partial_s X_{s,t} + b_s\cdot\nabla X_{s,t} = 0$, with $X_{s,s} = \mathrm{id}$.
  The squared residuals are the LMD and EMD losses, and their finite-difference
  versions DLMD and DEMD converge to them after division by $\delta^2$.
* Consistency distillation is DEMD with $t = 1$ and a stop-gradient; latent
  consistency models apply it to the guided ODE of a latent diffusion model;
  CTM is DEMD with a general destination time and a stop-gradient.
* The stop-gradient fixes the more accurate point and makes the loss a
  bootstrapped regression whose fixed point is the teacher's multi-step
  solution.
* In the parametrization $X_{s,t}(x) = x + (t-s)F_{s,t}(x)$, $F$ is the
  average velocity, $F_{s,s} = b_s$, and the Eulerian loss on the diagonal is
  flow matching. Adding that term gives the bootstrapped loss a stable target
  grounded in data.

## Connections and Further Reading

**Within the course.** @prp-learn and @cor-fm are the flow matching objective
of the earlier lectures on flow models, and the linear interpolant
$I_t = (1-t)x_0 + tx_1$ is the path used by rectified flow. Part I of this
slide deck (progressive distillation, denoising diffusion GAN) is the
pre-history of the methods here: progressive distillation also trains a
student to reproduce several teacher steps in one, but for one fixed pair of
times per stage. The next part of the deck continues with MeanFlow, which
trains the average velocity $F_{s,t}$ of @eq-avgvel directly from an identity
closely related to @eq-residual-F, and with flow map matching, which also
trains flow maps directly from the interpolant, without a pre-trained
teacher.

The FID values in @fig-timeline are those shown on the lecture slide. All
figures in this note were drawn for it; @fig-schematic redraws the
schematic of the slides, and the figures of the papers that the slides show
are described in the text rather than reproduced.
